items.stem: A GDC displays 4.8E−6. What number does this represent?
items.markingKey: 4.8 × 10⁻⁶. E stands for "× 10 to the power".

items.stem: Without converting to ordinary numbers, explain which is larger: 3.8 × 10⁻³ or 4.6 × 10⁻⁴.
items.markingKey: R1 compare powers first: 10⁻³ is ten times 10⁻⁴; since 4.6 < 10 the number 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ < 1 × 10⁻³ ≤ 3.8 × 10⁻³. A1 3.8 × 10⁻³ is larger.

items.stem: Felix writes: "A negative power of ten makes the number negative, so 4 × 10⁻² is negative." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: 10⁻² = 0.01 is positive; 4 × 10⁻² = 0.04 is a small positive number. A negative number has a minus sign in front of a.
items.markingKey: 10⁻² = 0.01 is positive; 4 × 10⁻² = 0.04 is a small positive number. A negative number has a minus sign in front of a. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Which of the following best describes "scientific notation (standard form)"?
options: The smallest value that a rounded measurement could have had before it was rounded
The power of ten k when a number is written in the form a × 10ᵏ, used to compare sizes roughly
The number a, with 1 ≤ a < 10, that multiplies the power of ten in a × 10ᵏ
Writing a number as a × 10ᵏ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and k is an integer
items.answer: Writing a number as a × 10ᵏ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and k is an integer
items.markingKey: D. "scientific notation (standard form)" is writing a number as a × 10ᵏ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and k is an integer.

items.stem: Which of the following is written in the form a × 10ᵏ, 1 ≤ a < 10, k ∈ ℤ?
items.markingKey: C. Only 7.02 × 10⁻³ has 1 ≤ a < 10 and an integer power.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The power of ten k when a number is written in the form a × 10ᵏ, used to compare sizes roughly"?
options: order of magnitude
estimation
mantissa (coefficient)
upper bound
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of order of magnitude.

items.stem: Explain why, after multiplying 6 × 10⁵ by 4 × 10³, the result 24 × 10⁸ must be adjusted.
items.answer: The coefficient 24 is not between 1 and 10; 24 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10⁹.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The coefficient 24 is not between 1 and 10; 24 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10⁹. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "5.6 × 10⁻³ is larger than 2.1 × 10⁻² because 5.6 is larger than 2.1." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Compare the powers first: 10⁻² is ten times 10⁻³, so 2.1 × 10⁻² = 0.021 > 0.0056.

items.stem: Briefly explain why scientific notation is useful when recording the masses of planets and of atoms.
items.answer: The numbers are extremely large or small; a × 10ᵏ shows the size (order of magnitude) at a glance, avoids long strings of zeros and makes the number of significant figures clear.

items.markingKey: R1 multiply the coefficients and add the powers; R1 adjust the coefficient so that 1 ≤ a < 10; A1 8.57 × 10¹⁶.

items.stem: Lars writes: "3.0 × 10⁴ + 2.0 × 10³ = 5.0 × 10⁷ because you add the numbers and the powers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Powers are only added when multiplying. For addition write both with the same power: 3.0 × 10⁴ + 0.2 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁴.

items.stem: 878 students from a school in Manchester travel to a sports event. Each bus holds 49 passengers and costs 511 GBP to hire. (a) Find the number of buses needed. items.answer: (a) 18 (b) 10.48 (c) rounding to the nearest integer could leave students without seats

items.stem: Explain why intermediate values in a calculation should not be rounded before the final answer.
items.answer: Rounding early introduces errors that accumulate through later steps, so the final answer may be wrong at 3 s.f.; keep full GDC values and round only at the end.

A room in Geneva is 9.35 m long, 4.72 m wide and 2.65 m high. The four walls are to be painted with 2 coats; one tin covers 10 m². (a) Estimate the wall area by rounding each dimension to 1 significant figure. (b) Calculate the wall area, correct to 3 s.f. (c) Find the number of tins that must be bought, justifying your rounding.
items.markingKey: (a) 2(9 + 5) × 3 = 84.0 m² (M1 A1). (b) 2(9.35 + 4.72) × 2.65 = 74.6 m² (M1 A1). (c) 2 × 74.6 ÷ 10 = 14.9 (M1); round UP since part of a tin cannot be bought and the walls must be covered: 15 (A1 R1).

items.stem: A room in Lisbon is 6.7 m long, 6.31 m wide and 2.44 m high. The four walls are to be painted with 1 coat; one tin covers 10 m². (c) Find the number of tins that must be bought, justifying your rounding.
items.markingKey: (a) 2(7 + 6) × 2 = 52.0 m² (M1 A1). (b) 2(6.7 + 6.31) × 2.44 = 63.5 m² (M1 A1). (c) 1 × 63.5 ÷ 10 = 6.35 (M1); round UP since part of a tin cannot be bought and the walls must be covered: 7 (A1 R1).

items.stem: To find the upper bound of a − b, which combination is used?

lower bound of a − lower bound of b
upper bound of a − lower bound of b
lower bound of a − upper bound of b
items.answer: upper bound of a − lower bound of b
items.markingKey: C. The difference is largest when a is as large and b as small as possible.

items.stem: Explain why the upper bound of a measurement of 12 cm (nearest cm) is 12.5 cm even though 12.5 would round to 13.
items.answer: The upper bound is the boundary of the interval 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5; values arbitrarily close to 12.5 round to 12, so 12.5 is the least upper bound, although it is not itself included.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a number less than 1 has a negative power of ten in scientific notation.
items.answer: To move from a (between 1 and 10) to a number less than 1 the decimal point moves left, i.e. a is divided by a power of ten: ÷ 10ⁿ = × 10⁻ⁿ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To move from a (between 1 and 10) to a number less than 1 the decimal point moves left, i.e. a is divided by a power of ten: ÷ 10ⁿ = × 10⁻ⁿ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why rounding 3 249 to 2 significant figures gives 3 200 and not 32.
items.answer: Rounding must preserve place value; the zeros are place holders that keep the number in the thousands.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rounding must preserve place value; the zeros are place holders that keep the number in the thousands. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a percentage error of 2% may be acceptable in one context but not in another.
items.answer: Acceptability depends on purpose: 2% on the length of a garden fence is negligible, but 2% on a drug dose or engineering tolerance could be dangerous.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Acceptability depends on purpose: 2% on the length of a garden fence is negligible, but 2% on a drug dose or engineering tolerance could be dangerous. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "5.6 × 10⁻³ is larger than 2.1 × 10⁻² because 5.6 is larger than 2.1." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Compare the powers first: 10⁻² is ten times 10⁻³, so 2.1 × 10⁻² = 0.021 > 0.0056.
items.markingKey: Compare the powers first: 10⁻² is ten times 10⁻³, so 2.1 × 10⁻² = 0.021 > 0.0056. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: M1 estimate (20 × 8) ÷ 0.5 = 320; R1 2740 is about ten times too large, so a key was mis-entered (true value 274).

items.stem: Explain why the percentage error uses the absolute value of v_A − v_E.
items.answer: Percentage error measures the size of the error relative to the exact value; whether the approximation is too big or too small does not matter, so the modulus is taken.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Percentage error measures the size of the error relative to the exact value; whether the approximation is too big or too small does not matter, so the modulus is taken. items.stem: A room in Cape Town is 9.34 m long, 5.84 m wide and 3.02 m high. The four walls are to be painted with 2 coats; one tin covers 12 m². (a) Estimate the wall area by rounding each dimension to 1 significant figure. (b) Calculate the wall area, correct to 3 s.f. (c) Find the number of tins that must be bought, justifying your rounding.
items.markingKey: (a) 2(9 + 6) × 3 = 90.0 m² (M1 A1). (b) 2(9.34 + 5.84) × 3.02 = 91.7 m² (M1 A1). (c) 2 × 91.7 ÷ 12 = 15.3 (M1); round UP since part of a tin cannot be bought and the walls must be covered: 16 (A1 R1).

items.stem: Nia runs 400 m (to the nearest metre) in 56.1 s (to the nearest 0.1 s). (a) Find the upper and lower bounds of Nia's average speed. (b) Nia claims an average speed of at least 7.11 m s⁻¹. Determine whether the claim is certainly true, justifying your answer.
items.answer: (a) LB 7.115 m s⁻¹, UB 7.145 m s⁻¹ (b) yes, since LB > claim
items.markingKey: (a) LB = 399.5 ÷ 56.15 (M1) = 7.115 (A1); UB = 400.5 ÷ 56.05 (M1) = 7.145 (A1). (b) R1 even the lower bound exceeds the claimed value, so the claim is certainly true.

items.stem: Radio signals travel at 3.00 × 10⁵ km s⁻¹. On a given day Venus is 1.48 × 10⁸ km from Earth and Saturn is 1.21 × 10⁹ km from Earth. (a) Find the time, in seconds, for a signal to reach each planet, in the form a × 10ᵏ. (b) A command is sent to a probe at Saturn and the reply returns to Earth immediately. Find the total time in minutes, correct to 3 s.f. (c) Find the difference between the one-way times, in the form a × 10ᵏ seconds.

A room in Dubai is 6.98 m long, 5.17 m wide and 2.91 m high. The four walls are to be painted with 2 coats; one tin covers 15 m². (a) Estimate the wall area by rounding each dimension to 1 significant figure. (b) Calculate the wall area, correct to 3 s.f. (c) Find the number of tins that must be bought, justifying your rounding.
items.markingKey: (a) 2(7 + 5) × 3 = 72.0 m² (M1 A1). (b) 2(6.98 + 5.17) × 2.91 = 70.7 m² (M1 A1). (c) 2 × 70.7 ÷ 15 = 9.43 (M1); round UP since part of a tin cannot be bought and the walls must be covered: 10 (A1 R1).

items.answer: The power of ten k when a number is written in the form a × 10ᵏ, used to compare sizes roughly

items.answer: The largest value that a rounded measurement could have had before it was rounded (the boundary itself is not reached)

items.stem: "A negative power of ten makes the number negative, so 4 × 10⁻² is negative." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 10⁻² = 0.01 is positive; 4 × 10⁻² = 0.04 is a small positive number. A negative number has a minus sign in front of a.
items.markingKey: 10⁻² = 0.01 is positive; 4 × 10⁻² = 0.04 is a small positive number. A negative number has a minus sign in front of a. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "An answer of 4.5 is the same as 4.50 when giving answers to 3 significant figures." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Their values are equal but 4.50 claims accuracy to the hundredths; to 3 s.f. the zero must be written: 4.50.
items.markingKey: Their values are equal but 4.50 claims accuracy to the hundredths; to 3 s.f. the zero must be written: 4.50. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The mass of a bar of soap is 397 g and its volume is 40 cm³, both to the nearest whole number. Explain which bounds of mass and volume give the upper bound of its density, and find it.
items.markingKey: R1 density = mass ÷ volume is largest for the largest mass and smallest volume; M1 397.5 ÷ 39.5; A1 10.06 g cm⁻³.

items.stem: Two lengths are 31 cm and 15 cm, each to the nearest cm. Freya says the upper bound of their difference is (31.5 − 15.5) = 16 cm. Explain why this is wrong and find the correct upper bound.
items.markingKey: R1 the difference is greatest when the first length is largest and the second smallest; M1 31.5 − 14.5; A1 17 cm.

items.stem: "3.0 × 10⁴ + 2.0 × 10³ = 5.0 × 10⁷ because you add the numbers and the powers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Powers are only added when multiplying. For addition write both with the same power: 3.0 × 10⁴ + 0.2 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁴.
items.markingKey: Powers are only added when multiplying. For addition write both with the same power: 3.0 × 10⁴ + 0.2 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁴. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: (a) Estimate the value of (69.5 × 5.84) ÷ 0.66 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure. (b) Use your GDC to find the exact value correct to 3 significant figures.
"Percentage error is (exact − approximate) ÷ approximate × 100%." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The denominator is the exact value: ε = |v_A − v_E| / |v_E| × 100%.

items.stem: A room in Nairobi is 9.64 m long, 5.57 m wide and 2.93 m high. The four walls are to be painted with 2 coats; one tin covers 12 m². (a) Estimate the wall area by rounding each dimension to 1 significant figure. (b) Calculate the wall area, correct to 3 s.f. (c) Find the number of tins that must be bought, justifying your rounding.
items.markingKey: (a) 2(10 + 6) × 3 = 96.0 m² (M1 A1). (b) 2(9.64 + 5.57) × 2.93 = 89.1 m² (M1 A1). (c) 2 × 89.1 ÷ 12 = 14.9 (M1); round UP since part of a tin cannot be bought and the walls must be covered: 15 (A1 R1).

items.stem: The radius of a circular pond is 7.2 m. Omar estimates its area using π ≈ 3 and the radius rounded to 1 significant figure. (a) Find the estimate. (b) Find the exact area correct to 3 s.f. (c) Calculate the percentage error and comment on whether the estimate is suitable for ordering pond liner.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × 7² = 147 (A1). (b) π × 7.2² = 163 (M1 A1). (c) |147 − 163| ÷ 163 × 100 (M1) = 9.74% (A1); R1 too large an error – an under-estimate would leave the pond uncovered.

561 students from a school in Zurich travel to a sports event. Each bus holds 52 passengers and costs 652 CHF to hire. (a) Find the number of buses needed. (b) The total cost is shared equally; find the cost per student correct to 2 decimal places. (c) Explain why the answer to (a) is not found by rounding to the nearest integer.
items.answer: (a) 11 (b) 12.78 (c) rounding to the nearest integer could leave students without seats
items.markingKey: (a) 561 ÷ 52 = 10.8 (M1) → 11 buses (A1). (b) 11 × 652 ÷ 561 = 12.78 (M1 A1). (c) R1 all students must be seated, so always round up.
